text: This session is recorded and your manager reads the derived record. Start with the dedupe store: why a Postgres table instead of Redis?

Two reasons. A dedupe record has to survive a restart, and Redis lost keys on failover in our setup. The table was also already in our backup rotation. Redis would have been faster, and my teammate Dev made exactly that argument: at peak, 300 events a second, he thought the table would add latency we'd feel. I measured it instead and the table was 4 milliseconds at p99 on that load, so his concern was real but not binding.
What's the key on that table, and what happens when the same event arrives a day later?

Partner id, claim id and event version, under a unique index. A day later the insert hits the unique violation and I treat that as a duplicate: log it, drop it, acknowledge the message. I didn't have to special-case time because the key has no time component.
What if the partner resends with the version number reset?

That actually happened. A partner resent a month of events with version 1 on every record. The index rejected them, which was the right outcome, but the rejection raised a page and woke me up twice. I moved known partners to a daily digest. What I'd do differently is add the replay allowlist before launch, not after the second page.
How did you know the stream output was right?

A two-week shadow period. We ran the stream next to the nightly file and diffed them each morning. By day nine there were zero unexplained differences; the early ones were ordering and a timezone bug in one partner's timestamps. Forty thousand events a day, so the diffs were a few dozen rows at first.
What breaks first at ten times the volume?

The dedupe table's write path. Every event is an insert with a unique check, so at 3,000 a second I'd expect index contention on the hot partner. I'd partition by partner id and batch the inserts, and I'd move the already-seen check to a bloom filter in front so only maybe-new events reach Postgres.
